name: wv_0003
text:
The drawing is a fragment with two wavy lines, so it has two attachment points.

The ring is a benzene. Its top-right carbon carries a quaternary carbon, which is bonded to a methyl group (the plain line going right). That carbon has a wavy line crossing the bond on its left side, where it joins the ring. A second wavy line sits on the bond going up and to the right, from the carbon toward the top. The wavy lines are drawn at the bond from the ring carbon to the CH carbon and at the bond from that carbon going down-right. The drawing therefore shows a carbon with three substituents: the aryl ring, a methyl, and one more wavy bond.

In the image, the central carbon at about (335, 68) has:
- a line to the left, to the ring at (285, 65), crossed by a wavy line,
- a line to the right, to the methyl at (385, 45), which is plain,
- a wavy line going down-right to (375, 60).

The wavy bonds are therefore the one crossing the ring-to-carbon bond and the one going down-right. Taking the methyl as plain, the carbon is CH(CH3) with two attachment points, one on the ring side and one on the other wavy bond. Written as the carbon with its ring, methyl and attachment point: *C(C)c1cc(Cl)ccc1F, plus a second * for the other wavy line, which would make the carbon *C(C)(*)... However, the wavy line crossing the ring-to-carbon bond marks the attachment of the ring-bearing carbon to the rest of the molecule, and the other wavy line is the continuation of the same bond type. I read this as a single attachment point on the ring-to-carbon bond, giving a 1-arylethyl group, with a second * on the carbon.

The ring numbering: the carbon bearing the side chain (C1) is adjacent to the carbon bearing F (C2) and, on the other side, to a CH next to the carbon bearing Cl. Cl is at the top-left carbon, which is meta to C1 across the ring, so Cl is at position 5 and F at position 2.

Final SMILES, with two attachment points on the central carbon:

SMILES: *C(*)(C)c1cc(Cl)ccc1F

name: wv_0011
text:
The drawing is a fragment with two attachment points, one at the wavy line and one at the open bond on the ring nitrogen.

**Ring:** a pyrazole. N1 carries a bond to the right that is cut off (an attachment point, likely a methyl or a larger group). N2 is the "N" at the top left, double-bonded to C3. C3 carries the chain substituent. C4 and C5 follow, with a double bond between C4 and C5 as drawn.

**Chain:** from C3 the chain runs down to a CH2 and then to a second CH2, which meets the wavy line at the bottom left. The wavy line is the other attachment point. The wavy line crosses a vertical bond, so the carbon at that position may be a branching carbon. The vertical wavy line sits at the junction where the chain ends, so I read it as the attachment on a CH2.

Tracing the chain: C3 connects up-left to a vertex, then down-left to a second vertex, then to the junction at the wavy line. That gives ring–CH2–CH2–*, with the wavy line crossing the bond at the end. The ring C3 attaches to a vertex at about (105, 97), then a vertex at (72, 155), then the wavy-line carbon at (15, 155). The wavy line is at x≈5, so the carbon at (15, 155) lies on it. That gives two CH2 groups followed by the attachment carbon. The carbon on the wavy line is a vertex with a bond to the left crossing the wavy line, so it is likely a CH2 as well, with the wavy line marking its other bond.

I will therefore write the chain as C3–CH2–CH2–*, with the ring N1 bearing a second *.

SMILES: *CCc1ccn(*)n1

name: wv_0013
text:
The drawing shows a cyclohexane ring in a chair conformation with two substituents, a left bond and a right bond. Each of these bonds is crossed by a wavy line, so each marks an attachment point.

Each wavy line crosses a bond close to the ring, and each bond continues past the wavy line as a short stub. The attachments could therefore be read as ring–CH2–* (a methylene between the ring and the attachment point) or as ring–* directly.

Checking the left side: the line runs from the far left at (3,72) to the ring at (130,105). The wavy line crosses it at about (65,90). The wavy line itself is a long vertical squiggle, from (80,25) to (50,150). The bond is therefore cut by the wavy line, and the line extending beyond it to the left is just the bond's continuation. The same holds on the right.

This makes the wavy line the attachment point, and the segment beyond it is part of the cut bond. The fragment is then *C1CCC(*)CC1, a 1,4-disubstituted cyclohexane.

The chair is drawn with the substituents at the 1,4 positions. The left substituent is on the lower-left vertex (130,105) and the right substituent is on the upper-right vertex (292,47). These are para to each other, so 1,4 is correct. No wedges or hashes are drawn, so I assign no stereochemistry.

SMILES: *C1CCC(*)CC1

name: wv_0015
text:
The drawing shows a 2,5-difluorophenyl ring attached to a quaternary carbon.

**Side chain.** The carbon attached to the ring has a methyl group and two wavy bonds. One wavy bond is drawn going up-left and the other down-right, both crossing bond ends. Each wavy line marks an attachment point, so the carbon carries two * atoms and one methyl.

The side chain is therefore *C(*)(C)Ar, with no stereochemistry.

**SMILES.** Writing the ring starting at C1: c1(C(*)(*)C) is attached to c(F) (C2), then cH (C3), cH (C4), c(F) (C5), cH (C6), closing back to C1. This gives *C(*)(C)c1cc(F)ccc1F, where the ring reads C1, C6 (H), C5 (F), C4 (H), C3 (H), C2 (F).

name: wv_0026
text:

name: wv_0022
text:
I read the image as a 1,2,3,4-tetrahydroisoquinoline: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered ring that contains one nitrogen. The nitrogen sits at position 2, bonded to two ring CH2 groups (C1 next to the aromatic ring, and C3 leading to C4).

The third bond from the nitrogen goes to a carbon drawn with two attachment points. One is a wavy line running down-left. The other is a bond running up-right that ends in a cut-off mark at the edge of the drawing, which I take to be a second wavy line. This part is the least certain. If the up-right line is only a stray mark, the substituent would instead be a single * on the nitrogen.

Reading both as attachment points, that carbon is a CH2 carrying two * atoms and bonded to the nitrogen.

name: wv_0027
text:
The drawing shows a tetrahydropyran ring (six-membered, with one O) attached at its 4-position to a quaternary carbon.

That carbon is where the wavy line crosses the bond. It carries one methyl, drawn as the line going right, and the ring. The wavy line appears to cross the vertical bond, which implies two attachment points: one at the top and one at the bottom of the wavy line.

On closer reading, the central carbon sits at the wavy line's crossing point. Its bonds go left to the ring, right to a methyl, up through the wavy line, and down through the wavy line. So the central carbon has four substituents: the ring, a methyl, and two attachment points, each marked *.

SMILES: *C(*)(C)C1CCOCC1

name: wv_0020
text:
The drawing is a 2,6-dimethylmorpholine ring cut at the nitrogen, with one wavy attachment line on N, so the SMILES has one `*` on N.

**Ring:** The six-membered ring contains N at the top right and O at the bottom left, with two CH2 groups and two CH(CH3) carbons. The CH(CH3) carbons flank the oxygen, so they are C2 and C6.

**Stereochemistry:** The methyl on C2 (upper left) is drawn with a wedge, and the methyl on C6 (bottom) is drawn with a hash.
- At C2, the priorities are O > CH2(N) > CH3. With the H pointing away, O → CH2 → CH3 runs counterclockwise on the page, so C2 is S.
- At C6, the priorities are the same. The hashed methyl puts the H toward the viewer, and O → CH2 → CH3 runs clockwise on the page. Reversing for the H gives counterclockwise, so C6 is S.

The result is (2S,6S), the trans isomer. I assigned `@` and `@@` in the SMILES below by working through the neighbour order at each stereocentre, and both give S.

SMILES: *N1C[C@H](C)O[C@@H](C)C1

name: wv_0029

The SMILES is therefore a 9-fluorenyl group with the attachment point on C9:

*C1c2ccccc2-c2ccccc12

Checking atom by atom: C1 is the CH carbon. It bonds to an aromatic ring (c2ccccc2) whose last atom is joined by a single bond to a second aromatic ring (c2ccccc12), and that ring closes back to C1. This gives the five-membered ring C9, two carbons of the first ring, and two carbons of the second ring.

name: wv_0028
text:
The drawing shows a pyridine ring attached at its 3-position to a sulfonyl group (S with two =O). The sulfur is bonded to a CH2, which is bonded to a carbon bearing a wavy line (the attachment point).

Reading the ring: N is at the top, and the carbon next to it on the right is bonded to the sulfonyl-bearing carbon, which makes the attachment position 3.

The line after CH2 ends at a vertex that has the wavy bond and a trailing "." mark. That vertex could be a carbon with the wavy line crossing a bond, so I read it as CH2 attached to a carbon that carries the wavy line. The drawing then has S–CH2–C(*), where the carbon is joined to the wavy line. The wavy line crosses a vertical bond, so the vertex is a carbon with a bond up and a bond down. That gives two attachment points on this carbon, but only one wavy line is drawn. Following the instruction of one * per wavy line, the fragment is pyridine-SO2-CH2-*.

Checking the geometry: the CH2 sits at the end of the S bond going up-right, and the vertex at the right is where the wavy line meets the CH2 bond. The wavy line is drawn vertically, and the bond from CH2 meets it at the middle. The carbon at that junction is the attachment atom itself. Taking the wavy line as crossing the bond from CH2 to the next atom, the fragment is *CS(=O)(=O)c1cccnc1.

SMILES: *CS(=O)(=O)c1cccnc1

name: wv_0030
text:
The drawing shows a pyrazole ring attached through N1 to a quaternary-looking carbon. Two things need reading carefully: the ring, and the wavy line.

**Ring.** It is a five-membered ring with two adjacent nitrogens. The left nitrogen (N) is double-bonded to a carbon, and the right nitrogen is the one bonded to the carbon above. The remaining ring bonds are C=C at the bottom right, so this is a pyrazol-1-yl group.

**Attachment.** From the ring N, a bond goes up to a carbon. A wavy line crosses at that carbon, running left to right through it, and a short line extends upward from it as a methyl.

The wavy line is drawn across the carbon itself, with the carbon sitting in the middle of it. That means the wavy line marks two attachment points, one on each side of the carbon. The carbon therefore carries two * attachments, a methyl, and the pyrazolyl group.

SMILES for the fragment: *C(*)(C)n1cccn1

Check on the ring: n1cccn1 has N1, then three carbons, then N, closing back to N1. The N–N bond is the ring closure, so the ring has two adjacent nitrogens as drawn.

SMILES: *C(*)(C)n1cccn1

name: wv_0033
text:
The drawing shows a benzene ring with a methyl group at one end (the line at upper left). At the lower right, the ring carbon connects to a wavy line. The wavy line passes through the bond end, so it marks the single attachment point. The ring is therefore a p-tolyl group with one attachment.

The wavy line seems to cross a short bond from the ring and extend on both sides. Counting the vertices, the bond leaves the ring at the lower right and reaches a point, which is where the wavy line crosses it. The wavy line runs from the lower left to the upper right, and the bond from the ring ends at its middle. The attachment point is therefore directly on the ring carbon, giving the p-tolyl fragment with one *.

SMILES: *c1ccc(C)cc1

name: wv_0031
text:
The drawing is a bicyclic fragment: a pyrazole fused to a pyrrolidine ring, i.e. 6,7-dihydro-5H-pyrrolo[1,2-b]pyrazole, with one attachment point.

**Pyrazole ring (5 atoms):** N (left, double-bonded to CH), N (top, bearing the ring fusion), the fusion carbon C3a, the carbon C3 carrying the wavy bond, and the CH at the lower left.
- N= is bonded to CH.
- CH is bonded to C(*).
- C(*) is double-bonded to the fusion carbon.
- The fusion carbon is bonded to the other N.
- That N is bonded back to N=.

**Pyrrolidine ring:** the N, CH2, CH2, CH2 and the fusion carbon. N is bonded to CH2 (top), then CH2, then CH2 (right), which is bonded to the fusion carbon.

**Bonds:** the double bonds are N=CH and C(*)=C(fusion), with the other bonds single.

SMILES: *C1=C2CCCN2N=C1

This reads atom by atom as:
- C1(*) bears the attachment point and is double-bonded to C2, the fusion carbon.
- C2 continues through CCC to N2, which closes the five-membered pyrrolidine ring back to C2.
- N2 is bonded to N, which is double-bonded to CH, which closes ring 1 back to C1(*).

SMILES: *C1=C2CCCN2N=C1

name: wv_0032
text:
The drawing is a fragment with a quaternary carbon on the left. This carbon has two wavy bonds, which are attachment points, plus a plain line going to the lower left, which I read as a methyl group. It also bonds to the CH2CH2 chain that leads to the piperazine.

Going through the pieces:

- The quaternary carbon carries two wavy bonds (two * atoms), one methyl, and the chain.
- The chain runs from the quaternary carbon to a CH2, then another CH2, then the piperazine N.
- The piperazine has a second N bearing a methyl, which is the line extending to the right at the top.

The central carbon is therefore C(*)(*)(C)CC–N. The line at the lower left ends at a free vertex, so it is a methyl.

SMILES: *C(*)(C)CCN1CCN(C)CC1

name: wv_0034
text:
The drawing shows an isoquinoline ring system. A CH2 group is attached to C1, the carbon next to the ring nitrogen. The wavy line is on the bond from that CH2 to the rest of the molecule, so it marks the single attachment point.

The wavy line sits on a bond that leads to a carbon with no label. That carbon is attached to the CH2, which in turn attaches to the isoquinoline C1. The wavy bond runs from the left edge to a vertex at about (75, 105). From there a bond goes up to (100, 75) and then to C1 at (155, 105).

Reading the vertices again, the wavy line crosses the bond between the left-hand attachment and the vertex at (75, 105). That vertex is the CH2, and it bonds to C1. The vertex at (100, 75) is the same CH2 as I counted a moment ago. So the chain is * – CH2 – C1 of isoquinoline, and the wavy line crosses the bond to the CH2.

The isoquinoline ring is C1(=N)…: C1 is bonded to N, and N is bonded to C3, which is bonded to C4 and then to C4a. The benzo ring is fused at C4a and C8a, and C8a is bonded to C1.

SMILES: *Cc1nccc2ccccc12

name: wv_0036
text:
The drawing shows a fragment: O connected to two CH2CH2 chains, each ending at a quaternary carbon. Each quaternary carbon carries a methyl (the line extending outward) and two wavy-line attachment points.

Reading the left side: the quaternary carbon sits at about (60, 62). A line runs from it up-left to (0, 30), which is a methyl. A wavy line runs up-right and another runs down-left. A plain bond runs down-right to (115, 95), then down to (115, 160), then to O. So the chain is C(quaternary)–CH2–CH2–O.
